facts.text: Borough Park was originally called Blythebourne, a cottage community built in 1887 by developer Electus B. Litchfield, who named it from the Scottish words for 'happy home.'
In 1902, developer William Reynolds bought land north of Blythebourne, subdivided it into 400 lots, and renamed the area Borough Park — marketing it as a suburban escape from city noise and dirt.
The elevation of the New Utrecht Avenue rail line after World War I — now the D train — spurred rapid growth in Borough Park, drawing Jewish families from the Lower East Side and Williamsburg.
Borough Park is home to one of the largest Orthodox Jewish communities outside of Israel, with nearly 300 synagogues and 50 yeshivas concentrated in the neighborhood.
Borough Park earned the nickname 'baby boom capital' of New York City, recording 4,523 births in 2004 — the highest of any neighborhood in the city that year.

Thirteenth Avenue is Borough Park's commercial spine, stretching roughly a mile from 39th to 55th Streets and lined with kosher markets, Judaica shops, and bakeries that draw visitors from across the city and beyond.
